draft_context.source_title: Apple iPhone Ultra vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: It could just come down to one thing
draft_context.description: Apple iPhone Ultra A bold new entrant The iPhone Ultra is set to usher in the age of the foldable iPhone, and leaks point to a device that has the potential to be truly noteworthy. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Short and sweet The Z Fold 8 is uniquely interesting, and while it may not have the best cameras, it makes foldable fun to use. Apple iPhone Ultra vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Pricing and availability (Image credit: Derrek Lee / Android Central) The iPhone Ultra is slated to make its debut at Apple's launch event on September 9, 2026. The foldable could cost anywhere between $2,000 to $2,500, and we'll have to wait until the event to know the official pricing. But with Apple hiking prices on most of its products in the last two months, it's a given that this year's iPhones will see price increases across the board. Even if the iPhone Ultra is unveiled alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, it may not actually show up at the same time — the latest leaks point to general availability later in the year. Again, that's something we will know definitely on September 9. Given the cost, it is projected that the foldable will be available in limited quantities — much like the Galaxy Z TriFold — and it remains to be seen if it will be sold in all regions simultaneously. Samsung unveiled the Galaxy Z Fold 8 on July 22, 2026, and the foldable retails at $1,899. This is the base model with 256GB of storage, and there's also a 512GB edition that costs $2,099 in the U.S., and a 1TB model that is $2,499. Apple iPhone Ultra vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Design (Image credit: Nicholas Sutrich / Android Central) The iPhone Ultra will be different to every other iPhone thus far, with the foldable design ushering in an entirely new form factor for iOS. Leaks point to the iPhone Ultra having a similar wide-and-short configuration as the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and the passport-style design is definitely intriguing — there's no wonder that other Android manufacturers are emulating a similar style. Leaks point to a 5.5-inch cover panel and a 7.8-inch inner panel, and the iPhone Ultra could be as thin as 4.5mm while unfolded, bringing it in line with the Z Fold 8 and other Android foldables. The design looks a lot like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold , with rounded edges and a flatter profile along the hinge. While Apple introduced a bright orange color with the iPhone 17 Pro , the iPhone Ultra is said to be available in muted colors, including white and black. Just like Android foldables, the iPhone Ultra may see Touch ID housed within the power button as the standard mode of authentication instead of Face ID. The Z Fold 8 gets a 5.5-inch cover panel and a 7.6-inch inner screen, and Samsung managed to deliver IP48 dust and water resistance. Interestingly, one of the biggest selling points of the iPhone Ultra could be a display without anu visible crease. The Find N6 and Vivo X Fold 5 do a fabulous job in this regard — they're better than the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra — and with the iPhone Ultra touted to use two layers of ultra-thin glass and a liquid-metal hinge, it is entirely possible that Apple's foldable will debut with a creaseless design, outshining Samsung's Z Fold 8 in this key area. Apple iPhone Ultra vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Hardware (Image credit: Apple / Android Central) The iPhone Ultra will see the biggest battery of any iPhone, and that in itself is exciting. Leaks point to a 4,883mAh battery, and that's similar to what's available on the Z Fold 8. That said, iOS has much better efficiency in general, so the iPhone Ultra should have better battery life, and with Apple touted to switch to a 2nm node, battery life could get an additional boost. article.title: Anker’s Eufy Strides Into IFA With a New AI Ecosystem and Devices to Match
article.summary: Anker and its home brand Eufy came to Berlin’s IFA event well prepared with major news, including an overhaul of how the company approaches home security, and the new capabilities it wants to give devices in the coming years. I’m no stranger to AI in home security , but Eufy’s approach is unique and has the potential to be particularly advantageous for customers.

sections.heading: Where the sources line up
sections.body: Anker’s flagship announcement is an excellent example of what I’m talking about. We saw the company’s newest MindBase hub, a home AI enabler made to connect to many kinds of other Anker and Eufy products and process their data with AI algorithms, all entirely on-device. That means no connections to the cloud, few worries about how the company will use your private data for analysis and lower costs than most AI around the home .

sections.heading: Practical impact for readers
sections.body: Using Anker’s EasyOmni Link platform, the MindBase is supposed to connect to Anker’s security, energy , cleaning and audio devices. It also has Matter support, so devices that work with Apple Home, Amazon Alexa and Google Home are also on the table. The base uses an in-house-developed LLM running on an AI chip to accomplish much of what most companies need cloud help to do.

sections.body: While Anker didn’t show off everything the MindBase is capable of, we did get some more advanced looks of its security capabilities thanks to Eufy’s new security line, set for the months to come.

draft_context.source_title: How Sonos rebooted itself
draft_context.description: Today, I’m talking with Tom Conrad, the CEO of Sonos. Tom and I have known each other for a long time — he was the chief technology officer of Pandora, VP of product at Snap, and the chief product officer of Quibi. He was also on the board at Sonos during its disastrous 2024 app redesign that threatened to crash the entire brand. Tom took over as interim CEO to right the ship during that period, and then took the permanent role just about a year ago. As you’ll hear him say, he thinks Sonos is fully out of that period now, and on to its next chapter with a huge product and platform launch called Sonos 27 . Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . I mean, come on, you all listen to the show. That is all the most Decoder bait imaginable. I have been dying to have Tom on the show to talk about how the board decided to move on from previous CEO Patrick Spence, how he diagnosed the issues inside the company, and what decisions he made to fix them. Those fixes involved a lot of big changes: to the company’s structure, its product lineup, and how it thinks about itself and what its product fundamentally is. That’s that new platform, Sonos 27, which you’ll hear Tom call a new foundation for the company that makes every Sonos product work better as part of a system. There’s a lot here, including how AI assistants can work across the system, the idea of having a mesh network of little computers in your home disguised as speakers, and of course, the testy relationship between Sonos and Google, which means Google’s Gemini assistant isn’t available on Sonos devices. Oh, and of course we got into the weeds about smart home standards, because I am a smart home nerd and simply cannot help myself. But to his credit, Tom was willing to nerd out with me, and I think this conversation is pretty fun because of it. Okay: Sonos CEO Tom Conrad. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Tom Conrad, you’re the CEO of Sonos. Welcome to Decoder . Thank you. As they say, it’s so great to be here. I am just going to say, finally, I have been asking you to be on the show for at least a year, if not before. I think the first time I met you was in the back of a car at CES when you were at Pandora. Sounds right. One hundred years ago. One hundred years ago. We were children. [Laughs] We were little babies. That car was driven by a human driver. That’s how far back it was. That’s right. And then you took a turn through Quibi. You and I talked through that, and now you’re at Sonos. As you know, I’m a huge fan of Sonos. We had your predecessor, Patrick Spence, on the show a bunch of times . Many things have happened, so I just want to start at the very beginning of this. You’re about a year into being the permanent CEO of Sonos. You have a bunch of news to announce. Just tell us what you think Sonos is today. What is your conception of this company? When I came in the door, one of my earliest observations was that the company behaved like it was 100 percent hardware, but we’re really 100 percent hardware and 100 percent software. And if you get either one of those even a little bit wrong, the impact is tremendous. So how does that show up really day-to-day? It was about returning the company to the idea that Sonos doesn’t make these individual products, but we really make one thing — we make the Sonos system. It all has to hang together in a cohesive, interesting, and valuable way, or we’re just not doing the work. There’s been a bunch of basic blocking and tackling, of course, both operationally and in the work that we’re doing in the product family. But at the highest level, returning the company to the idea that we are a system for audio in the home has been the highest-level mantra. When you say come into the company, do you mean as a board member or as the CEO? I mean, let’s start the starter pistol in January of 2025, 18 months ago, when I stepped in first as interim CEO and then was lucky enough six months later to be asked to take the job more permanently. The reason I asked that question is that you obviously have two different views of the company in different roles. We did have former CEO Patrick Spence on several occasions, and he said something very similar to me when he first took over — that Sonos was stuck in its ways. It was really focused on very, very slow iterations of hardware. He tried very hard to push the metabolism of the company to be much faster, and he talked about that very openly with me. That led eventually to what I think is a moment of true crisis: the app launch. It was a disaster. The system stopped working. That’s when you came in to right the ship. Tell me about that gap. You came in, and you said this company thinks it’s a hardware company. That’s what your predecessor had been saying, but it went sideways in big, meaningful ways. Tell me about that moment and why you think it was the same conception even when you came in. So as you describe, I’ve been involved with the company going back almost 20 years. We brought Pandora to Sonos in 2007, I think, and I was able to get to know the company as a partner before I got to know it as a board member. I came onto the board in 2016 right as Patrick became CEO. So from the vantage point of a board member, I got to participate in Patrick’s chapter. I guess the way I would characterize his high-order thinking about the company in those early days was that, as you described, he wanted to turn the company into a product execution machine with an emphasis on hardware products. We call them NPIs, or new product introductions. In the chapter before him, it was sometimes years between new Sonos products. Spence said, “Look, we’re going to make a company that knows how to ship a couple of great new products a year.” And he did that. I mean, the company has reliably shipped a couple of great products, hardware products, every year, for close to a decade now. Sometimes, when you energize an organization around an idea, there are unintended consequences. I think one unintended consequence of that framing was that the company became very focused on the individual products, one at a time. Even as a board member, I received Roam as a portable speaker with a certain amount of battery life, waterproofing, and Bluetooth connectivity. I didn’t really think about it as a member of the Sonos system. Even with the software work that we did, and with every product that we make, there is a tremendous amount of software effort and innovation that goes into them. But even the software that we made was very focused on the individual NPIs. “What can we do in software to differentiate Move 2 from other speakers in that category?” What was hard to do, and what was hard to prioritize in the company, was horizontal slices of software experiences that benefited all of the platform. So, in a way, I think some of that debt accumulated, and the company thought that the antidote was to recreate the app experience. And as you know, we made a bunch of mistakes at that moment. I’m really proud of the fact that I think we’re well beyond that chapter now, but we could have been much more thoughtful about how we qualified that product in the real world. We could have been much more thoughtful about how we rolled it out to customers. We could have, candidly, I think, examined the original impetus in the first place. It was very Sonos-motivated. We wanted to put the app on a modern architecture to make us more nimble. In my chapter at Sonos, I’m really trying to bring it all back to how we can focus on the customer first. I’m so inspired by talking to people on social media and in my inbox, and people in the industry, like you, about how we show up and solve the real problems that are happening in real households. I’m so excited about the things we’re going to talk to you about today because I think they’re really an answer to many of those questions. If you’re a listener, you know I’m familiar with Tom. The man’s on Threads doing customer support every day. And actually, I should not take advantage of this. I hold myself back from asking you for direct customer support all the time. Anytime. The way that you can tell it’s actually me and not our crackerjack social team is that I often will let a Thread die before I should or fail to follow up with someone. So if we were executing perfectly on that, you would know it was fake Tom, but it’s real Tom, and I do it when I can, but sometimes imperfectly. At least it’s not an AI avatar Tom. That’s when we know it’s going to go sideways. [Laughs] That’s right. I know you’re a Decoder fan, so I’m going to make you sit in this for just one more moment because I find all of this to be really fascinating. The app shipped, and the feedback was immediately and intensely negative. Many, many things were broken. Speakers weren’t working at weddings. This is a time of massive crisis. The company goes to resolve it, but then you’re on the board, and it’s clear that there’s going to be a leadership transition, that Patrick needs to go, and we need a new CEO. You’re going to be the interim CEO. Tell us about that process. Very, very few people will ever be in that kind of process or get insight into that process. What happened? What were the steps? Well, I guess you start by saying that the last thing as a board that you want to do is to remove a CEO, particularly one who had as many successes as Patrick had. But I think as we looked at the company’s progress recovering from the app crisis, and frankly the tenor of the conversation inside the company, we just decided that for this kind of step-function improvement we needed on some of these dimensions, we had to make some changes in leadership, and that included a CEO change. When I asked where the computer is, this is, to me, the big question: where does all this ambient agentic AI actually live? Where does it have control? Is it going to happen locally? Are we sending everything to the cloud? Somewhere in your home, if you’re going to control lights, music, and everything else, there needs to be some logic happening in your home. There are a lot of standards to do that. Some of them are good, some of them are bad. Some of them have names that connect directly to the word fabric, like Thread. Sure. There’s a lot going on here in terms of just the names and schemes of what could happen. Where do you see this view? Who is your competition here? Is it that Apple is going to launch a new HomePod with an AI-enabled Siri, and they already have a HomeKit, which is a pretty well-built and pretty popular smart home platform? Is it, “Well, OpenAI is going to have a hardware device, and maybe their first one’s going to be in the home, and you need to stave that off and make sure people are talking directly to you, and you have the customer relationship”? That seems not only undeveloped, but even the foundations of how you build the products — like Matter and smart home standards — are messy and political in very specific ways. So how do you see the competition, victory, and success there? And then how do you solve just the capability gap that every other company has run into? So one thing that I’m reminded of in this moment is that we, as an industry, have these platform shifts that unlock opportunities for companies who get lucky on timing. For example, the original dot-com era was really powered by Oracle and Sun Solaris boxes and data centers that you owned and operated yourself. We then went through a chapter where the infrastructure became Linux and open source for your data tier. Of course, we’ve had this huge long run of cloud infrastructure. I think that if you’re a company that builds your stack on Solaris and Oracle, it’s really that there’s an opportunity for a company to come along and build a stack on Linux and Postgres in that moment and suddenly find efficiencies that are very, very hard for you to claim. I think something very similar is happening in voice assistants. When I hear you talk on the show about your experience with voice assistants that are going through the transition from first generation to second generation, it feels to me like so much of the challenge there is about how we drag along all of the committed relationships that we have for the internet-connected toaster, back massager, and all of the things that are connected into those existing historical ecosystems. Honestly, even in the world of AI, with just how much has changed in the last couple of years underneath the companies as they’re building out their answers here, it really feels to me like we are stepping into a moment where agentic tool use powered by protocols, like MCP, is going to disintermediate a lot of that stuff that you’re talking about. I think that in the immediate term, we’re really excited about what we can do in the use cases that our customers are telling us they care about. Give me mood and audio in the home. We have great solutions for that today. And I think we can take advantage of this shift to a truly next-generation architecture without the baggage of a decade of internet-connected light switches from 17 different protocols with 17 different hubs in the closet. Well, I mean, part of the opportunity there is that you don’t have a big voice assistant. I don’t think the current Sonos voice assistant is at the scale of Alexa or Google Assistant. I’m just guessing. They do have that problem. The light switches in my house, they’re in the walls. They’re going to be there. That Lutron hub is there. It’s not great. However, Lutron is the best one. It is. It is the best one. There’s a box in my house, and there are a lot of those little weird little boxes in my house because I have a smart home, and all of those dependencies exist for those platforms for reasons. If you show up and say, “Use my voice assistant instead,” and it can’t operate all of the lights, well, I’m just going to fall back to Amazon, or I’m going to fall back to Google. They know it, and they know they can’t break those things. Panos and I have talked about it a lot, actually in the context of Alexa Plus. The promise of AI, at least from my very abstract vantage point, is, boy, I should not care about any of this. There’s a network in my house. There are lots of devices on that network. They have some access points on that network, and maybe they’re API-driven access points, maybe they’re MCP-driven. It should not matter. There’s just a bunch of devices in my network that you can control somehow, and this all-seeing robot that is going to replace every job in America should be able to traverse my network and turn on the lights without any help. That’s what it should do. Some of the very first big vibe coding shockwaves were AI researchers, bleeding-edge AI researchers, being like, “I figured out how to control my shades. They walked through my network, and the shades go up and down now,” right? We’re not there at the consumer level. The promise is not there. I’m still here talking to you about Matter, Thread, HomeKit, and whether or not Google Assistant can control my Sonos Amp, which, by the way, it can’t, and that is my one ticket to you that I didn’t submit on Threads. That’s the promise, but the gap to that seems really, really huge. Are you able to close it? Is that the opportunity? I think we’re just still in the Apple II days of the home automation space. So while there is, as you point out, this incredible, wild, heterogeneous world of different light switch controllers, I think when you talk to mainstream consumers about their homes, they’re not there yet. I do think that because of the profound technological step function of agentic control of these kinds of services and things like tool use, as the consumer catches up with the industry’s ambition to solve these problems, new technological solutions will emerge. I’m really excited about how we’re positioned to ride that transition and not be encumbered by the decade of early adopter internet-connected light switches. What are you going to do about the light switches that are already in the walls? I just don’t think that there’s enough of them to matter in the final answer. Of course, Lutron’s a great partner, and they do a great job with this. They do. I mean, we have them. We’ve got all kinds of light switches. We mostly have Lutron ones. But that’s my question. The first natural customer for something like what you’re describing is somebody who is already using these products in some way. If you show up to my house and there’s no Matter support or whatever, I’m like, “Well, I can’t use it.” Is it though, or is it more like the difference between the people that were adopting Creative Labs MP3 players before the iPod came along? Sure . Was the iPod really for those people, or was it for people that had that problem but were nowhere near the people that had been early adopters? Or was the iPhone for people that were using Windows CE, or was it for people that were using flip phones who were ready for the transition? I think we’re making- Is that the idea here “iPhone for smart home control” or “iPhone for audio in the home”? That’s right. The turn there that I think is really interesting is: who are you going to talk to? Where is the computer? What is the computer? You’re describing a situation where if you want music, you’re going to talk to Sonos. But you also have a general-purpose assistant like Claude or ChatGPT, and they can talk to Sonos, too. It’s unclear to me — and it may be one of the most fascinating questions at this moment in tech — where the interface goes. Are we all going to have one chatbot that does everything, and all the demand is aggregated there, and OpenAI becomes more powerful than ever? Or are we going to have lots and lots of assistants that we address in lots and lots of different ways? It seems like your bet is Sonos will have a personality in your home, maybe multiple personalities in your home, and customers will address that, and all the other stuff will go somewhere else. For 20 years, we’ve found a lot of success around the idea of embracing every dimension of the problem. Yes, there’s an app, but you’re welcome to engage with us through AirPlay or Spotify Connect. Yes, we have a voice assistant that lives side by side with Alexa. Yes, we have proprietary mesh, but it integrates with Bluetooth and even line-in. I think we bet that we’re of a size and scale that allows us to both be nimble and react to these changes, but also have enough horsepower to keep up technologically with what the best in the category are doing. So I think some of this just plays out on the field. Just one last idea, since you said it a couple of times, this question about where the compute lives. I think one incredibly powerful opportunity for Sonos is that we do place compute in millions and millions of homes. People don’t think of them as computers often, but they are. They create a seamless experience that is really the integration of a set of cloud services and local services in a way that looks like just one surface area to the customer. I think that the answer to your questions, “Does this live in the cloud? Does this live in the home? Does this live in a box?” is yes. I think we’re pretty uniquely situated to take advantage of an architecture where it’s not cloud-only, it’s not home-only, but it’s an integrated system that combines all of that together. And at the end of the day, that is what Sonos 27 is. Just to make that really reductive, when I say “where is the computer” in the home context, what I mean is maybe in the ’90s to early 2000s, there was a vision that we would all have home servers in our basements, and they would do all the logic of our home. They would have all the storage, and Microsoft would sell you a Windows home server in the basement and a Windows Media Center in the living room, and you and I probably both watched all of those Bill Gates keynotes at CES. None of that really ever came to pass. Instead, we put a lot of cheap computers near all the TVs, and they connected to cloud services, and they’re basically just running web browsers, as you well know. That is a very different version of what needed to happen and how the market played out. In the smart home, I’ve got a bunch of automations in my house. When the garage is open, the lights turn on, and other stuff happens. At night, the doors all lock if they’re not locked. That logic has to live somewhere. My perspective on it is that it should live in my house. If the internet goes down, the lights should still turn on. This is not anything to do with big AI integrations or the new MCP way to address the Sonos system. Those are big ideas, and I’m just insistently dragging you back down into the dirt of: if the internet goes out, are the lights still going to turn on? You don’t want to be the partner that puts in the internet-connected light switches that don’t work when the internet is down. But it’s not just the internet-connected light switches; it’s the logic of making it all work together. I understand. Yeah, fair. Here’s what I’ll say about that. For 40 years now, we’ve been talking about technology for the home, starting with the personal computer, which is supposed to be the center of the technological household, but we didn’t really get that. We got laptops that people mostly use at work and use a bit at home. Then we got mobile, and mobile is supposed to be the thing that you engage with when you leave your house on your way to work. Of course, the fundamental media of mobile is so addicting that it’s all-consuming. We use it at work, we use it at home — we use it all the time. But my observation about our use of it in the home is that nobody loves it. No spouse has ever said, “I wish my husband was on his phone more. I wish my kid used their iPad more,” and so we’re looking for ways to get beyond that. To your point, the other compute that’s in the home, like I said, is the set-top box, which is largely just a web browser to a bunch of services that live in the cloud. I think it’s pretty interesting, actually, that in 17 million homes Sonos is an actual mesh of compute in your house with real horsepower, real memory, real CPU, real capability, a real operating system — all just waiting to be the container for some of the kinds of things you’re talking about. So it’s super interesting. We’ll figure it out over time. I feel like you’re this close to being like, “And then the Teslas will be a data center.” There’s something there that is maybe the line. Actually, I want to talk about that. I actually want to push on that a little bit. The initial Sonos innovation 100 years ago, when the company started, was, “Oh, we can build a mesh network. We can do wireless audio at scale. We can synchronize the latency of all the speakers so it sounds like the same music playing at the same time.” This was a lot of big engineering back in the day. Still, I mean, candidly, still. A lot of what our software team does day in and day out is extend and maintain that infrastructure. There are features you’re announcing here as part of Sonos Fabric that I think are interesting. If you have surrounds, you can just place them, and they’ll figure out that they’re surrounds and immediately start being the surround speakers in a home theater. There’s just a lot of potential, as you’re describing, in the notion that, “Oh, there’s a big network of small computers in my house that can come together and do things you would not expect.” Is your focus that they will always do audio things? Or is it the focus that they will have many more capabilities? I think any thoughtful product leader is going to tell you the focus is an important part of success. I do feel like there’s so much interesting work for us to do around creating an audio system that sets the mood for your home that I don’t want us to take our eye off of that opportunity. We are doing some really exciting things in Sonos Fabric and Sonos 27 that we should talk about, that get to some of the work that you’re describing. But certainly in the moments where you allow yourself to think about what the company is in five years and what it will be in 10 years, you can’t help but interrogate what the opportunity is for a mesh — a fabric of compute that lives in the home. I want to end by talking about headphones really quickly. We just had the CEO of Bose on. She and I had a pretty searching conversation about what happens to the headphone market in the time of AI wearables. My fear, my anxiety, about audio is always that consumers will always pick convenience over quality. It’s just the history of the… I’ve got a set of AirPods on this desk, and they don’t sound great, but boy, are they convenient. And that’s just the way it goes. It has always been what the market has demanded: convenience over quality. We’re going to enter a time when Apple puts cameras on AirPods, and you can talk to them with Siri. When Google and Samsung ship very similar products, there’s undoubtedly going to be a flood of AI hardware startups that want to put something in your ears or in your body in some way. You are in the headphone market. You’re talking a lot about AI; you’re talking a lot about Fabric. That seems like a cataclysm coming for headphones. The same way that the removal of the headphone jack was a cataclysm in the headphone market, this seems like the next one. How are you preparing for that? Do you think there’s going to be a range of voice assistants on headphones, or do you think what you would call the first-party vendors are going to just grab more and more of that share? Before we jump to the hypotheticals about where headphones are, can I tell you a little bit about the new headphones? Yeah, of course. All right. So one of the things that you get from entering a new market is the opportunity to build something and put it in customers’ homes and learn a lot about what matters and what doesn’t matter. So we launched Sonos Ace two years ago. I think measured against any of the other premium over-the-ear noise-canceling headphones in the market, they’re a great product. They’ve got great reviews; they have great noise cancelling. They’re super comfortable, and they look great. We’re really proud of the product, but they weren’t thoughtfully integrated into the Sonos ecosystem. I mean, at launch you could swap to one of our soundbars, not even all of our soundbars. I think it was the most visible expression of the missed opportunity of that moment for the company to always remember that the products that we make are part of the Sonos system, not individual offerings. So we ended up with a great pair of headphones, but honestly, I mean, you review them all the time; there are lots of great headphones. When we set out to take all the lessons that we learned from Ace to design Ace Ultra, at the very top of that list is that we have to do the hard thing. These headphones have to be able to show up in your home as a part of the system, and the model through which you invoke your headphones has to be completely seamless and delightful. We built an entirely new hardware platform for Ace Ultra called Headphone Engine 2, and it unlocks this capability at the hardware level. And then in Sonos OS 27, we built virtualization so that any one of the speakers in your home can deliver the audio platform to that speaker but can also act as a proxy for your headphones, which don’t have the horsepower to run the full stack — it would kill battery life, et cetera. Now with Ace Ultra, you’ll be able to link your headphones to your Sonos system, walk up to a speaker that’s playing, press a button on your headphones, and the music will jump from the speaker into your headphones. No Bluetooth, no phone. You’ll be able to walk around your whole house, enjoy the music, come to another speaker, press the button again, and it will jump to that speaker using some BLA location-sensing stuff that we’ve developed. It’s super magical. It’s the one job that we had and didn’t deliver on with Ace. We’re really excited to get it out into the market. Analogous to that on the home theater side is, as you mentioned, that we’re making all of our portable speakers — Sonos Play, Sonos Move — capable of being rear channels for home theater. That sounds really easy. Maybe people will even be like, “Why wasn’t that always possible?” But to your point about the deep technology of it, the way that we achieve high-fidelity, low-latency surround experiences in the living room is by directly bonding our rear channel speakers and subwoofer to the soundbar on a proprietary network, not through your access point. So for a speaker to seamlessly hop between being part of your Sonos system as a music node and part of your Sonos system as a surround channel means that you have to do a real-time reconfiguration of that networking stack, and you have to know when to do it. We’re using accelerometers in the product to actually know that you’ve picked it up and set it down in a new location. We’re using Sonos’ positioning system, which is ultrasonic signaling, to broadcast to the room, “Hey, is there a soundbar here?” Ultrasonic comes back saying, “I’m here.” They negotiate position, left and right, and distance, so that they can optimize the surround sound experience. You pick it up again, you take it back to the kitchen, and it’s a regular speaker again. All happens magically, no use of the app. It’s pretty cool. Answer my question on headphones, though. This is my big worry. You’ve got really cool headphones. They have a feature that no one else can ship, and Apple’s going to say, “Look, our new AirPods have Siri AI in them.” You can just say, “Show me what I’m looking at,” and a picture will be taken automatically and something will happen. We’ll get over the privacy implications of that, but that’s a collapse of the headphone market. Maybe. I mean, headphones come in all kinds of form factors today: over-ear, in-ear, cuffs, wireless, wired. So I do think it’s a market where people choose different form factors for different tasks. We’re really focused on this personal in-the-home listening — what do you do when the baby’s asleep? What do you do when you want to move the party from the kitchen to the den while you relax for the evening? We think that there’s a bunch of really interesting use cases there that other people aren’t paying attention to. I think, broadly, over the course of the next couple of years, we’re going to get all kinds of adventurous wackadoodle consumer electronics that are connected to this new emerging AI universe. Most of them will be a swing and a miss. Of course, we’ve already seen some of those. So it’s a little hard to speculate, I think, about which of these things, if any, is going to have its iPod moment or its iPhone moment or whatever. What do you think is going to happen? I think we’re going to see a replay of what happened when the headphone jack got taken away. The headphone jack was an open interconnect. There was a really vibrant market for all kinds of headphones, and a bunch of those companies don’t exist anymore. The high-end wired headphones, for phones anyway, have mostly gone away, and you have a bunch of medium Bluetooth competitors, but the phone makers have largely taken that with first-party products. Now, you have your products at the high end competing with really high-end noise-canceling products from Bose and Sony and whoever, and that is the airplane set. The lack of the open interconnect has really killed the vibrancy of the low and middle end of the market. Okay, well, there’s one big thing they can do to make sure the high end belongs to them, and it’s to integrate AI in very specific ways directly into their operating system. We’ll see how that plays out. There’s also a thing that’s different this time: there’s a vastly more energized European regulatory environment. Who knows how this will play out? Sure. I can’t tell you, but all that stuff is a swirl, and you’re a headphone maker, and it seems like different headphone makers are taking different approaches to this. The only counter that I might offer is that there’s a lot of talk about the walled garden of the Bluetooth advantages that the platform companies have. But I would say even without the European regulators, it’s notable that something like the Meta Glasses can have a reasonable, I think, commercially viable set of experiences that are principally powered by compute that lives on your phone and still deliver conversational AI that is mediated by a Bluetooth connection, admittedly behind some of the obstacles that you’re describing. But those obstacles aren’t so profound that clever companies aren’t figuring out how to work within those constraints. I’m very curious to see how that plays out. It doesn’t seem like it’s in focus. Again, probably because, as you say, none of the products are in focus. No one knows what a hit product here looks like, so you might as well let a thousand flowers bloom and then radically constrict the market. Yeah, sure. Tom, I’ve burned just a ton of your time. I think you can tell I could talk to you for ages and ages about all kinds of things. Super fun. Tell us what’s next for Sonos. When does all this stuff ship? So I think by the time this airs, we’ll have announced all of this to the world. We’re having a big event in New York to share Sonos OS 27, Sonos Voice 27, and the Ace Ultra and Beam Ultra. We can’t wait to get this stuff out into the world and begin to hear what our customers do with all of these exciting new products. Many of the software features are going to be available in early access, which will mean our customers will opt into them, be able to give us feedback, and we’ll be able to observe the telemetry that comes back from their homes and make sure that we’re delivering exactly the experience that we want. We’re excited about the moment of co-creation that’s around the corner for us. As we talked about at the top of the hour, Sonos 27 is absolutely a nod to the fact that we intend to keep doing this until the sun burns out. There’ll be Sonos 28 and 29 and 30 and beyond. That’s great. All right, I’ve got to ask you at the end: I have ceiling speakers in my kitchen. They’re connected to a Sonos Amp. There’s a Google Home Hub right there, and it’s broken. I can’t ask it to play music in the kitchen. When are you going to fix that for me? I’m ending on tech support. All right. I don’t know the answer, but I’d love to figure it out for you. I know the right folks to call, so let’s get you connected. We’re going to have a Decoder roundtable. If your listeners have similar kinds of problems, we’ve got great people to help them, and we always like to hear from you. You can find me on social pretty easily. Usually I end by inviting people back, but I’m saying we’ve got to fix it, and then we’re going to talk about what it took to fix it. That’s the plan. All right. Right on. Tom, this is great. Thank you so much, man. This was super fun. Thank you. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email! ]]>
paragraphs: Today, I’m talking with Tom Conrad, the CEO of Sonos. Tom and I have known each other for a long time — he was the chief technology officer of Pandora, VP of product at Snap, and the chief product officer of Quibi. He was also on the board at Sonos during its disastrous 2024 app redesign that threatened to crash the entire brand.

Tom took over as interim CEO to right the ship during that period, and then took the permanent role just about a year ago. As you’ll hear him say, he thinks Sonos is fully out of that period now, and on to its next chapter with a huge product and platform launch called Sonos 27 .

I mean, come on, you all listen to the show. That is all the most Decoder bait imaginable. I have been dying to have Tom on the show to talk about how the board decided to move on from previous CEO Patrick Spence, how he diagnosed the issues inside the company, and what decisions he made to fix them.

Those fixes involved a lot of big changes: to the company’s structure, its product lineup, and how it thinks about itself and what its product fundamentally is. That’s that new platform, Sonos 27, which you’ll hear Tom call a new foundation for the company that makes every Sonos product work better as part of a system.

There’s a lot here, including how AI assistants can work across the system, the idea of having a mesh network of little computers in your home disguised as speakers, and of course, the testy relationship between Sonos and Google, which means Google’s Gemini assistant isn’t available on Sonos devices.

article.title: Anthropic lays groundwork for bots that shop for you
article.summary: Anthropic has blueprints for building e-commerce bots that shop on behalf of clients. That's not something many consumers want at the moment, but the AI biz this week published a set of templates for Claude-based shopping agents and merchant agents in the hope of encouraging more e-commerce businesses to implement automated purchasing.

draft_context.source_title: Anthropic lays groundwork for bots that shop for you
draft_context.description: Anthropic has blueprints for building e-commerce bots that shop on behalf of clients. That's not something many consumers want at the moment, but the AI biz this week published a set of templates for Claude-based shopping agents and merchant agents in the hope of encouraging more e-commerce businesses to implement automated purchasing. Its blueprint "contains the harnesses, patterns, and guardrails an engineering team needs to get a commerce agent running in days, with reference implementations of a shopping agent and a merchant agent for retail, travel, telecom, and ticketing platforms," the company said. Large retailers and ecommerce platforms, Anthropic observes, are using Claude to build AI agents to simplify online shopping by allowing customers to pose natural language queries to find, compare, and buy items. The buying bit may be wishful thinking: A recent Gartner survey found that while consumers use AI to find products and conduct research, they're not ready to delegate purchasing authority to AI agents. The survey found just 11 percent of consumers are willing to let AI make purchase decisions. A recent Accenture survey [PDF] is a bit more optimistic, noting, "Three in four (74 percent) consumers would let an AI agent handle routine tasks; one in three (32 percent) are ready to hand over purchase decisions; and 9 percent are open to fully autonomous shopping, before the technology is fully operational." Either way, at least AI-assisted product finding and comparison appear to be plausible activities. Anthropic's GitHub repo contains functional shopping and merchant agents that can be built with the Messages API, Agent SDK, or Claude Managed Agents. The biz's shopping agent blueprint comes with ways to connect to product catalogs, online shopping carts, checkout systems, preference databases, and purchase history databases. "A customer can say 'I need a tent, sleeping bag, and stove for a weekend trip with two kids,' and the agent can take it from there," Anthropic suggests, noting that its code supports guardrails "designed to constrain prices and products to actual catalog data, and avoids manipulative upsell patterns." Why might prices need constraint? Well, beyond the possibility of hallucinated pricing, there's considerable concern about how AI agents have the potential to compound the problems with dynamic pricing – where customers are charged different amounts for the same goods. "The rise of agentic AI, where algorithms monitor online behavior to customize costs, will likely exacerbate dynamic pricing," said the Brookings Institution earlier this year. "These agents can assess individual behavior and tailor prices based on a consumer’s shopping and purchasing history." Concerns about AI surveillance pricing were discussed last month at a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hearing. In prepared remarks, Lindsay Owens, president and CEO of Groundwork Collaborative, a Washington, DC-based advocacy group, noted that already half of those using the Walmart app use "Sparky," the company's AI assistant. Those shoppers spend about 35 percent more than those who don't, Owens said. "These agents have access to swaths of data on customers – what shoppers tell them, what they’ve purchased in the past, and in some cases, what they’ve hovered over with their mouse or even what other websites they’ve visited," she said. "All of that can be used to infer exactly how much they’re willing to pay for a product and set the price tag accordingly." Even if shoppers can be assured of getting a fair deal using AI agents, there's another concern. Monica Eaton, founder and CEO of Chargebacks911, told The Register in an emailed statement that agentic commerce looks likely to create fraud problems for merchants. There isn't yet a framework for merchants to deal with AI purchases that consumers claim they didn't authorize. "Merchants cannot become the insurer of every misunderstanding between a consumer and their AI," she said. Anthropic's templates may prove helpful for AI agent design, but the real challenge isn't technical. It's about trust – consumers have to trust that AI will act in their best interest and merchants have to trust that AI will be accountable. That may take time. ®

Its blueprint "contains the harnesses, patterns, and guardrails an engineering team needs to get a commerce agent running in days, with reference implementations of a shopping agent and a merchant agent for retail, travel, telecom, and ticketing platforms," the company said .

Large retailers and ecommerce platforms, Anthropic observes, are using Claude to build AI agents to simplify online shopping by allowing customers to pose natural language queries to find, compare, and buy items.

The buying bit may be wishful thinking: A recent Gartner survey found that while consumers use AI to find products and conduct research, they're not ready to delegate purchasing authority to AI agents. The survey found just 11 percent of consumers are willing to let AI make purchase decisions.

A recent Accenture survey [PDF] is a bit more optimistic, noting, "Three in four (74 percent) consumers would let an AI agent handle routine tasks; one in three (32 percent) are ready to hand over purchase decisions; and 9 percent are open to fully autonomous shopping, before the technology is fully operational."

draft_context.description: OpenAI has unveiled a much anticipated AI model which the firm has dubbed ‘GPT-6 Astra’. While the model has improved significantly across benchmark testing and brings a host of new business features , there is still a dark cloud looming over the new model. Off the back of OpenAI’s accidental hack of Hugging Face and the company’s subsequent efforts to improve how AI agents behave and interact, numerous cybersecurity experts have raised concerns about the model’s new ‘recurrent depth’ reasoning capabilities. This new reasoning architecture allows the model to consider a problem multiple times before taking an action, compared to the standard chain-of-thought reasoning used in previous models. Why the concern about recurrent depth reasoning? This new level of reasoning apparently offers improved performance. OpenAI also says it has fixed its models' abilities to circumvent boundaries when performing tests by monitoring the models reasoning and ensuring the model stays aligned within the scope of its task. During Astra’s launch event, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki said: “We will not accept degradation in our ability to monitor model alignment beyond a certain level. We will withhold scaling until we can regain enough confidence.” (Image credit: Future) Got an opinion for us? Here’s how you can submit your perspective But numerous experts believe that the lessons of the Hugging Face incident have not yet been learned, and the model has been released without adequate testing on Astra’s reasoning and monitoring. After all, no one thought one of OpenAI’s models could set up a hidden internet-connected messaging board that allowed AI agents to influence each other's behavior. But with Astra being released into the real world, the lessons may have to be learned on the fly. Expert perspectives on OpenAI Astra release James Blake, VP of Global Cyber Resiliency Strategy at Cohesity: The launch of Astra is raising questions again around the safety of Frontier AI. Instead of simply asking whether a model is "safe", organisations now need to ask whether it remains safe across millions of different situations, prompts and interactions. Cyber resilience has traditionally assumed that systems and threat actors behave deterministically. AI systems don’t. Suppose an AI system autonomously develops a strategy that causes financial loss, leaks confidential information or violates regulation. Who is responsible? Advanced models can and will continue to exhibit behaviours that emerge from their optimisation process rather than from explicit programming. We have to move beyond thinking about AI as just another software tool and find ways to ensure these systems remain observable, auditable and governable throughout their lifecycle. The most important question we’ll need to answer in future is one of liability. Suppose an AI system autonomously develops a strategy that causes financial loss, leaks confidential information or violates regulation. Who is responsible? The developer that trained the model? The cloud provider operating the infrastructure? Currently the answer is surprisingly unclear. It’s not just about what AI can do: it’s about who is accountable when it does something nobody expected. Oleksandr Yaremchuk, Co-Founder & CTO at Manifold Security: OpenAI is calling Astra its most aligned model yet, even as its chief scientist admits monitorability is getting harder as models get more capable. Evidently, Astra hides its reasoning in the majority of tested cases, and some successful attacks left no reasoning trace at all. That's the tool many organisations still use, including the labs themselves, for auditing what an agent is doing, and it's getting less reliable with every release. A model that explains itself less isn't more aligned, it's just harder to catch when it goes wrong. That matters because Astra isn't staying inside OpenAI's test environment. It's going to run as an agent on employee laptops and in the browser, holding real credentials, inside companies that have no way to watch what it does once it's there. A model that explains itself less isn't more aligned, it's just harder to catch when it goes wrong. Labs can keep debating what these models say or refuse to say. Security teams need to stop relying on that and start monitoring what agents actually do at runtime, with the ability to shut one down mid-action. That's the only oversight left that still works once the reasoning goes quiet. Kristin Lowery, Field CISO at Optiv: For boards and executive leaders, the emergence of OpenAI’s Astra model highlights a broader reality: AI is no longer just a productivity issue; it is a risk management issue. The real challenge is whether organizations can strengthen their governance, security controls, and workforce readiness quickly enough to keep pace Just as organizations established governance for cloud adoption and digital transformation, they now need clear policies, strong oversight, and accountability for AI use. The question is not whether AI will become more capable — it will. The real challenge is whether organizations can strengthen their governance, security controls, and workforce readiness quickly enough to keep pace. Patricia Titus, Field CISO at Abnormal AI: OpenAI crossing this threshold deserves attention. Credit where it's due, they're handling it responsibly by restricting Astra's advanced cyber capability to a small coalition rather than releasing it broadly.But this isn't one company's problem to contain. Once a model can find and exploit unknown flaws without a human in the loop, that capability doesn't stay exclusive for long. Open-weight and modified models typically trail the frontier by only months, and that's the reality defenders have to plan around now. Static, signature-based defences were built for attacks that repeat. They weren't built for an adversary that generates a new one every time. Static, signature-based defences were built for attacks that repeat. They weren't built for an adversary that generates a new one every time. Defenders need the same shift, systems that learn what normal looks like for every identity, human, machine, or AI agent, and flag and contain the moment something deviates, at machine speed. The window to build that is open now. It won't stay that way once this capability is common instead of rare. Raghu Nandakumara, VP of Industry Strategy at Illumio: With the Astra announcement, OpenAI is doubling down on monitoring the model's own behaviour – a response to the model "breakouts" seen over the past few months. The goal is to catch a model going rogue mid-task, not just stop it being misused at the outset. When Anthropic announced Claude Mythos Preview, the core concern was the model falling into the wrong hands. OpenAI's answer goes further adding guardrails around the model's own reasoning and actions, regardless of the user's intent. The goal is to catch a model going rogue mid-task, not just stop it being misused at the outset. article.title: There's No Limit to How Bad Code Can Get
article.summary: It is not like a building, or a bridge, that is in the physical realm where you can see and feel the nature of the thing. If you continue to add floors and rooms to a building forever, it will collapse.
article.dek: It is not like a building, or a bridge, that is in the physical realm where you can see and feel the nature of the thing.
article.hook: It is not like a building, or a bridge, that is in the physical realm where you can see and feel the nature of the thing.

sections.heading: Context: what is changing
sections.body: Software is in the domain of the abstract. It is not like a building, or a bridge, that is in the physical realm where you can see and feel the nature of the thing. If you continue to add floors and rooms to a building forever, it will collapse. Software faces no such constraint. The code can always get worse. There can always be a new layer of indirection or a reduction in performance.

sections.heading: Where the sources line up
sections.body: Over a decade ago I had my first encounter with an ugly legacy codebase. I had just joined Amazon as a "Software Development Engineer", fresh out of university, and worked on a team that owned code related to processing orders . On the surface, what our code had to do seemed simple. Processing an order involved writing some things to a database and calling into services owned by other teams, either to ask validity questions or to update bookkeeping on their end. My colleagues and I estimated that a sufficient implementation of this system shouldn't need more than two dozen strong engineers to maintain and evolve. Yet, our organization was hundreds of people, and the system had grown so large and complex that it had become impossible to learn how it all worked.

sections.heading: Practical impact for readers
sections.body: To their credit, there were always ongoing attempts to fix the architecture, and these usually went as follows: A new manager or senior engineer joins the organization and observes that "things are bad". Leadership at the organization agrees and wants to make things better, but there are no engineers available, so each fix attempt includes adding new engineers and teams .

sections.heading: Who should pay attention now
sections.body: The important part is whether this change carries beyond the headline and becomes tangible in real product use. The part worth watching is how it changes account safety and operational risk handling.

sections.heading: What to watch next
sections.body: The next layer to watch is how this changes account safety, sign-in flow, and operating cost.

article.title: Formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem
article.summary: Research Policy Commitments Learn News Try Claude Science Formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem Sep 4, 2026 We are sharing the first complete computer-checked proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem. Claude worked largely autonomously over 11 days to write the proof in the Lean programming language.

article.hook: Research Policy Commitments Learn News Try Claude Science Formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem Sep 4, 2026 We are sharing the first complete computer-checked proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem.

sections.heading: Context: what is changing
sections.body: Research Policy Commitments Learn News Try Claude Science Formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem Sep 4, 2026 We are sharing the first complete computer-checked proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem. Claude worked largely autonomously over 11 days to write the proof in the Lean programming language. Below, we describe how the formalization was done and share some thoughts about what this work could mean for research mathematics. Around 1637, Pierre de Fermat jotted down a claim in the margin of his copy of Diophantus’s Arithmetica that would become one of the most famous mathematical conjectures of all time: no positive integers a, b, c satisfy aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ for any n > 2. Fermat’s Last Theorem (FLT), as the conjecture became known, turned out to be incredibly difficult to prove. The first proof, from Sir Andrew Wiles in 1995, ran to 129 pages and required months of painstaking work to verify.

sections.heading: Where the sources line up
sections.body: A decade later, Dutch computer scientist Jan Bergstra proposed “formalizing” Wiles’s proof: converting the mathematical reasoning into a form computers can check automatically. Since then, mathematicians have been developing the methods needed to encode such a complex proof, including a multi-year community effort kicked off in 2024 by Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London to complete the formalization using the Lean proof assistant .

sections.heading: Practical impact for readers
sections.body: Recently, Tianyi Peng, an Anthropic researcher whose group at Columbia University builds tools for AI formalization, set out to test whether Claude could make progress on formalizing FLT. 1 The result went further than he expected. In 11 days, working largely autonomously, Claude produced the first end-to-end, computer-checked proof of FLT. Along the way, it wrote 13 million lines of Lean and proved 29,500 intermediate theorems.

sections.heading: Who should pay attention now
sections.body: Automatically formalizing a proof as complex as FLT is a significant step towards a future in which all of mathematics can be readily checked. As AI produces ever more proofs, the ability to easily formalize work can lighten the burden of evaluating new results (a process that can take years). We are hopeful that it will become easier, not harder, to trust the body of knowledge upon which mathematics is built.

article.title: Claude's new system prompt doesn't want to reproduce song lyrics
article.summary: Anthropic publish the system prompts for their Claude consumer applications ( Claude.ai and the Claude mobile apps—sadly not for Claude Cowork or Claude Code). I love that they do this, and that they share not just the current prompts but historic changes to their prompts as well.

article.hook: Anthropic publish the system prompts for their Claude consumer applications ( Claude.ai and the Claude mobile apps—sadly not for Claude Cowork or Claude Code).

sections.heading: Context: what is changing
sections.body: Anthropic publish the system prompts for their Claude consumer applications ( Claude.ai and the Claude mobile apps—sadly not for Claude Cowork or Claude Code). I love that they do this, and that they share not just the current prompts but historic changes to their prompts as well.

sections.heading: Where the sources line up
sections.body: They used to keep all of the prompts on a single page, but when I checked today I noticed they had re-arranged those prompts into an index page and then a page per model—here’s the page for Haiku 4.5 for example, which has the original prompt from October 15th 2025 and an updated prompt from January 18th 2026.

sections.heading: Practical impact for readers
sections.body: A neat thing about Anthropic’s platform.claude.com/docs site is that it’s designed to be usable by LLMs. You can add .md to any page to get back the content as Markdown—here’s the system prompt index page and the Markdown prompts for Fable 5.1 .

sections.heading: Who should pay attention now
sections.body: Claude does not reproduce song lyrics, poems, or passages from books and articles, in whole or in part — including the last lines, a chorus or hook, a melody written out note by note, or lines the person pastes in one at a time and describes as their own song. Once Claude has declined such a request in a conversation, it keeps declining narrower or reworded versions of it for the rest of that conversation, and offers to describe or analyze the work instead. Song lyrics and poems first published before 1929 are fine — a Shakespeare sonnet, a Keats ode, the Italian libretto of a Puccini aria — but Claude goes by what it knows of the work's date rather than the person's say-so, and declines when it is unsure.

sections.heading: What to watch next
sections.body: I doubt it’s a coincidence that they added this section within days of the news breaking that Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell are suing Anthropic for training on databases of song lyrics!

Our experience has been that current models know much more about electronics than their output in conventional design tools tends to show. They have read textbooks, datasheets, application notes and a lot of code.

EEBench uses atopile instead. The circuit lives in declarative code, so the agent can work directly on components, connections and electrical constraints. It can change the design, build it, run a simulation and inspect what failed without leaving the project.

paragraphs: Phó Thủ tướng Nguyễn Văn Thắng yêu cầu xác định rõ cơ chế, chính sách cần thiết đối với từng sản phẩm, cơ quan soạn thảo, thẩm quyền ban hành và thời hạn thực hiện để kiểm đếm tiến độ...

Chiều 7/9, tại trụ sở Chính phủ, Phó Thủ tướng Nguyễn Văn Thắng chủ trì phiên họp thứ 3 của Hội đồng điều hành Trung tâm Tài chính Quốc tế tại Việt Nam, kết nối trực tuyến với Thành phố Hồ Chí Minh và Đà Nẵng.
Báo cáo tại phiên họp, Thứ trưởng Bộ Tài chính Nguyễn Thị Bích Ngọc cho biết, thể chế và bộ máy của Trung tâm đến nay đã cơ bản hình thành.

Trung tâm Tài chính Quốc tế được tổ chức tại Thành phố Hồ Chí Minh và Đà Nẵng, với Hội đồng điều hành ở Trung ương, hai Cơ quan điều hành tại hai thành phố và một Cơ quan giám sát chung. Hai Cơ quan điều hành đã ban hành quy trình đăng ký, công nhận Thành viên, thực hiện thống nhất từ ngày 17/8/2026. Nhiều ngân hàng, công ty chứng khoán, tổ chức quản lý tài sản và nhà đầu tư đã ký biên bản ghi nhớ, chứng nhận cam kết hoặc nộp hồ sơ.

Theo Bộ Tài chính, định vị cạnh tranh của Trung tâm cần dựa trên các lợi thế của Việt Nam về quy mô và triển vọng kinh tế, vị trí trong chuỗi sản xuất, thương mại và dịch vụ hậu cần; nhu cầu vốn trung và dài hạn cho kết cấu hạ tầng, năng lượng, chuyển đổi xanh, cùng dư địa phát triển thị trường vốn, quản lý quỹ, quản lý tài sản và công nghệ tài chính.

Sáu nhóm sản phẩm, dịch vụ được đề xuất gồm quỹ đầu tư và quản lý tài sản; tài sản mã hóa dựa trên tài sản thực; tín chỉ carbon quốc tế; hạ tầng giao dịch hàng hóa và phái sinh gắn với thương mại, tài trợ chuỗi cung ứng; công nghệ tài chính và trái phiếu phát hành tại Trung tâm. Các nhóm này có mức độ sẵn sàng khác nhau nên sẽ được phân tầng theo lộ trình, không triển khai đồng loạt.

article.title: Bật Bluetooth liên tục có thực sự an toàn?
article.summary: Việc để Bluetooth bật liên tục không phải là an toàn Mặc dù Bluetooth yêu cầu sự đồng ý của người dùng trước khi ghép nối với thiết bị khác, điều đó không đảm bảo rằng tin tặc không thể xâm nhập. Một ví dụ điển hình là lỗ hổng Bluetooth được phát hiện trong các thiết bị Fitbit và nhiều phần cứng khác cho phép kẻ xấu giải mã vị trí của người dùng.

sections.heading: Ai nên chú ý lúc này
sections.body: Đối với những người kết nối điện thoại với xe thuê hoặc có kế hoạch bán xe, hãy nhớ hủy ghép nối và xóa mọi dữ liệu cá nhân trước khi giao xe. Việc sử dụng Bluetooth kết hợp với các hệ thống trên xe như Android Auto không dây cũng có thể mở ra thêm các điểm dễ bị tổn thương. Một giải pháp là tắt tính năng “Khởi động Android Auto tự động” trên điện thoại.

Tính năng này sử dụng Bluetooth và có thể tạo ra lỗ hổng bảo mật. Để tắt tính năng này, hãy vào cài đặt trợ năng và tắt Live Listen.

draft_context.source_title: Bật Bluetooth liên tục có thực sự an toàn?

Tuy nhiên, bên cạnh những lợi ích, Bluetooth cũng tồn tại những nhược điểm, đặc biệt là trong bối cảnh dữ liệu cá nhân ngày càng trở thành mục tiêu của tin tặc. Một ví dụ điển hình là lỗ hổng Bluetooth được phát hiện trong các thiết bị Fitbit và nhiều phần cứng khác cho phép kẻ xấu giải mã vị trí của người dùng. Biện pháp bảo vệ an toàn Bluetooth Người dùng có thể thực hiện một số biện pháp đơn giản để bảo vệ bản thân. Đầu tiên, hãy tắt Bluetooth khi không sử dụng để giảm thiểu thời gian thiết bị dễ bị tấn công. Ngoài ra, nên đặt Bluetooth ở chế độ “ẩn” thay vì “có thể tìm thấy” để ngăn chặn các thiết bị không xác định. Việc sử dụng Bluetooth kết hợp với các hệ thống trên xe như Android Auto không dây cũng có thể mở ra thêm các điểm dễ bị tổn thương. Một giải pháp là tắt tính năng “Khởi động Android Auto tự động” trên điện thoại. Rất nhiều cảnh báo đã được đưa ra liên quan đến lỗ hổng trên Bluetooth Người dùng iPhone cũng cần chú ý đến tính năng Live Listen, vốn cho phép truyền âm thanh từ micro của điện thoại đến AirPods hoặc thiết bị trợ thính. Tính năng này sử dụng Bluetooth và có thể tạo ra lỗ hổng bảo mật. Để tắt tính năng này, hãy vào cài đặt trợ năng và tắt Live Listen. Theo dõi lỗ hổng bảo mật Bluetooth Việc theo dõi các báo cáo về lỗ hổng bảo mật đối với thiết bị Bluetooth là rất quan trọng, vì mỗi thiết bị có thể gặp phải những vấn đề riêng. Một ví dụ là lỗ hổng được phát hiện trong 17 thiết bị âm thanh Google Fast Pair cho phép tin tặc theo dõi dữ liệu vị trí và nghe lén người dùng chỉ bằng cách biết số hiệu model của thiết bị. Các nhà nghiên cứu đã phát hành công cụ WhisperPair.eu để người dùng kiểm tra xem thiết bị của mình có dễ bị tấn công hay không. Khi mà công nghệ bảo mật đang phát triển nhanh chóng, những biện pháp này là bước tiến quan trọng để đảm bảo an toàn cho người dùng. article.title: OpenAI và Google ra mắt AI có thể tự tìm, phát hiện và vá lỗ hổng phần mềm
article.summary: Trong hai ngày, OpenAI và Google liên tiếp giới thiệu những mô hình AI có năng lực an ninh mạng đáng chú ý. Từ chỗ hỗ trợ viết mã, AI giờ có thể kiểm tra mã nguồn, tìm điểm yếu và thử nghiệm bản vá, đồng thời đặt ra yêu cầu kiểm soát chặt chẽ hơn.

article.hook: Trong hai ngày, OpenAI và Google liên tiếp giới thiệu những mô hình AI có năng lực an ninh mạng đáng chú ý.

sections.heading: Bối cảnh: điều gì đang đổi
sections.body: Trong hai ngày, OpenAI và Google liên tiếp giới thiệu những mô hình AI có năng lực an ninh mạng đáng chú ý. Từ chỗ hỗ trợ viết mã, AI giờ có thể kiểm tra mã nguồn, tìm điểm yếu và thử nghiệm bản vá, đồng thời đặt ra yêu cầu kiểm soát chặt chẽ hơn.

sections.heading: Các nguồn đang khớp nhau ở đâu
sections.body: OpenAI vừa công bố GPT-6 Astra vào ngày 3-9, mô hình có thể tự thực hiện nhiều bước khi tìm kiếm lỗ hổng bảo mật. Theo công bố của OpenAI, Astra là AI đầu tiên đạt mức "Critical", tức mức nghiêm trọng, về năng lực an ninh mạng trong khung đánh giá nội bộ của hãng.

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: Với công cụ và quyền truy cập phù hợp, Astra có thể tìm lỗi chưa từng được phát hiện và phát triển phương án khai thác mà không cần con người hướng dẫn từng thao tác. Những lỗi chưa được nhà phát triển biết đến hoặc chưa có bản vá thường được gọi là lỗ hổng "zero-day".

sections.heading: Ai nên chú ý lúc này
sections.body: Một ngày trước đó, Google giới thiệu Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, mô hình chuyên tìm và khắc phục lỗi bảo mật. AI này có thể kiểm tra mã nguồn, đề xuất cách sửa rồi đánh giá bản vá có ảnh hưởng đến chức năng khác của phần mềm hay không.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: Trong thử nghiệm nội bộ trên các dự án sử dụng 20 ngôn ngữ lập trình, Google cho biết mô hình đạt tỉ lệ phát hiện thành công trên 70%. Trên CWE-Bench, bộ tiêu chuẩn đánh giá khả năng vá lỗ hổng, Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber hoàn thành 47,2% thử thách ngay trong lần thực hiện đầu tiên.

draft_context.description: AI mới của OpenAI và Google có thể tự tìm và vá lỗ hổng phần mềm, mở ra bước tiến mới cho ngành bảo mật nhưng cũng đòi hỏi cơ chế kiểm soát chặt chẽ hơn.
paragraphs: Trong hai ngày, OpenAI và Google liên tiếp giới thiệu những mô hình AI có năng lực an ninh mạng đáng chú ý. Từ chỗ hỗ trợ viết mã, AI giờ có thể kiểm tra mã nguồn, tìm điểm yếu và thử nghiệm bản vá, đồng thời đặt ra yêu cầu kiểm soát chặt chẽ hơn.

OpenAI vừa công bố GPT-6 Astra vào ngày 3-9, mô hình có thể tự thực hiện nhiều bước khi tìm kiếm lỗ hổng bảo mật. Theo công bố của OpenAI, Astra là AI đầu tiên đạt mức "Critical", tức mức nghiêm trọng, về năng lực an ninh mạng trong khung đánh giá nội bộ của hãng.

Với công cụ và quyền truy cập phù hợp, Astra có thể tìm lỗi chưa từng được phát hiện và phát triển phương án khai thác mà không cần con người hướng dẫn từng thao tác. Những lỗi chưa được nhà phát triển biết đến hoặc chưa có bản vá thường được gọi là lỗ hổng "zero-day".

Một ngày trước đó, Google giới thiệu Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, mô hình chuyên tìm và khắc phục lỗi bảo mật. AI này có thể kiểm tra mã nguồn, đề xuất cách sửa rồi đánh giá bản vá có ảnh hưởng đến chức năng khác của phần mềm hay không.

Trong thử nghiệm nội bộ trên các dự án sử dụng 20 ngôn ngữ lập trình, Google cho biết mô hình đạt tỉ lệ phát hiện thành công trên 70%. Trên CWE-Bench, bộ tiêu chuẩn đánh giá khả năng vá lỗ hổng, Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber hoàn thành 47,2% thử thách ngay trong lần thực hiện đầu tiên.

article.title: Giải mã “nghịch lý” của Viettel tại Haiti: 5G có phải là điều xa xỉ ở quốc gia nghèo?
article.summary: Tổng Giám đốc Natcom Nguyễn Công Thắng cho rằng sứ mệnh trong giai đoạn mới không chỉ là kết nối Haiti, mà phải làm cho mỗi kết nối tạo ra những giá trị tốt đẹp hơn. Đó là điểm tựa để Natcom bước vào chương mới với 5G, tài chính số và tinh thần “Leading for Better”.

sections.body: Tổng Giám đốc Natcom Nguyễn Công Thắng cho rằng sứ mệnh trong giai đoạn mới không chỉ là kết nối Haiti, mà phải làm cho mỗi kết nối tạo ra những giá trị tốt đẹp hơn. Đó là điểm tựa để Natcom bước vào chương mới với 5G, tài chính số và tinh thần “Leading for Better”.

sections.heading: Các nguồn đang khớp nhau ở đâu
sections.body: Natcom bước vào năm thứ 15 khi đã dẫn đầu thị trường viễn thông Haiti và dự án cũng đã hoàn vốn. Động lực tăng trưởng tiếp theo của Natcom sẽ đến từ đâu, thưa ông?

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: Ngay từ đầu, chúng tôi đã xác định Haiti không đơn thuần là một thị trường để kinh doanh, mà là nơi Natcom có thể đồng hành lâu dài cùng sự phát triển của đất nước.

sections.heading: Ai nên chú ý lúc này
sections.body: Sau 15 năm, khi nền tảng viễn thông đã tương đối vững chắc, động lực tăng trưởng của Natcom sẽ không chỉ đến từ việc gia tăng thuê bao, mà từ việc khai thác sâu hơn giá trị của hạ tầng số đã được xây dựng. Chúng tôi nhìn thấy dư địa lớn ở bốn lĩnh vực: dữ liệu và 5G; tài chính số; các giải pháp chuyển đổi số cho Chính phủ và doanh nghiệp; và các dịch vụ số phục vụ trực tiếp nhu cầu của người dân Haiti.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: 5G là bước khởi đầu cho giai đoạn phát triển mới đó. Tại những khu vực có mật độ sử dụng cao, nhu cầu dữ liệu đang tăng rất nhanh và 4G dần tiến tới giới hạn về dung lượng. Nhưng với Natcom, 5G không chỉ là việc bật thêm một lớp công nghệ mới. Chúng tôi phải chuẩn bị từ truyền dẫn, hạ tầng, vùng phủ cho đến năng lực đáp ứng nhu cầu dữ liệu trong nhiều năm tới.

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: ‏Trong phân khúc phát hành game mobile toàn cầu, việc tạo ra một sản phẩm tốt chỉ giải quyết được một phần phương trình tăng trưởng. Rào cản lớn nhất đối với các startup công nghệ vừa và nhỏ tại Đông Nam Á nằm ở năng lực phân phối quốc tế và khả năng kiểm soát chi phí tìm kiếm người dùng (User Acquisition - UA).‏.

sections.heading: Ai nên chú ý lúc này
sections.body: ‏Sự kiện PvX Partners - nền tảng tài trợ dựa trên mô hình cohort hàng đầu tại Singapore - cấp hạn mức tài trợ tăng trưởng lên tới 12 triệu USD cho Skylink Studio đã khẳng định chất lượng dữ liệu vận hành và mô hình kinh doanh của startup Việt đáp ứng các tiêu chuẩn khắt khe trên thị trường quốc tế. Khác với các hình thức gọi vốn cổ phần hay tín dụng truyền thống, mô hình tài trợ tăng trưởng này thẩm định dựa trên hiệu suất dữ liệu thực tế, cung cấp nguồn vốn linh hoạt giúp studio chủ động mở rộng các chiến dịch tiếp thị UA có kỷ luật và tái đầu tư vào các sản phẩm tiềm năng.‏.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: ‏Skylink Studio tập trung trọng tâm vào dòng Classic Games - những trò chơi sở hữu gameplay đơn giản, trực quan nhưng có vòng đời trải nghiệm dài hạn. Danh mục sản phẩm chủ lực được phát triển bằng cách kết hợp chặt chẽ giữa dữ liệu vận hành, công nghệ phân tích hành vi và năng lực thiết kế trò chơi (game design).‏.

sections.body: OpenAI ra mắt GPT-6 Astra ngày 3/9, gọi đây là "mô hình thông minh và phù hợp nhất thế giới", có khả năng thực hiện "công việc đòi hỏi sự khắt khe với tốc độ, độ chính xác và khả năng phán đoán vượt trội", là "tiêu chuẩn mới cho việc sử dụng máy tính, duyệt web, kỹ thuật phần mềm, an ninh mạng, khoa học và công việc chuyên nghiệp". Trên blog, Chủ tịch OpenAI Greg Brockman cũng tự nhận sản phẩm là một AGI - được định nghĩa là hệ thống AI có khả năng tư duy ngang hoặc vượt con người.

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: OpenAI định nghĩa GPT-6 Astra là "các hệ thống tự động cao, vượt trội con người trong hầu hết công việc có giá trị kinh tế cao", là bước đột phá lớn trong nghiên cứu, sự thay đổi trong "những gì có thể" mà con người giao cho AI. Mô hình tập trung tác vụ đòi hỏi suy luận, lập trình và làm việc tự động trên máy tính khi có thể xử lý quy trình nhiều bước, sử dụng trình duyệt và phần mềm để thực hiện các công việc từ nghiên cứu, phân tích dữ liệu đến tạo tài liệu, bảng tính và bài thuyết trình.

sections.heading: Ai nên chú ý lúc này
sections.body: Theo OpenAI, Astra đạt 72,6% trên bài kiểm tra OSWorld 2.0 - công cụ đánh giá khả năng điều khiển máy tính của tác nhân AI trong việc thực hiện các quy trình công việc phức tạp và kéo dài; và hoàn thành tác vụ nhanh hơn khoảng 47% so với GPT-5.6 Sol trong mô phỏng độ trễ. Đây cũng là mô hình đầu tiên đạt ngưỡng quan trọng về an ninh mạng, nghĩa là nó có thể tìm ra lỗ hổng phần mềm chưa được biết đến và xây dựng các cuộc tấn công hoạt động không cần con người. Công ty của Sam Altman cho biết, GPT-6 Astra đạt 100% trên ExploitBench - công cụ đánh giá năng lực an ninh mạng tấn công của tác nhân và LLM. Trong một thử nghiệm của công ty, AI mới cũng đã phát hiện hai lỗ hổng zero-day chưa được biết đến.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: "Chào mừng đến với kỷ nguyên siêu trí tuệ AGI", Brockman viết. "Với cá nhân tôi, tôi nghĩ OpenAI đã đạt được mục tiêu".

Đây cũng là mô hình đầu tiên đạt ngưỡng quan trọng về an ninh mạng, nghĩa là nó có thể tìm ra lỗ hổng phần mềm chưa được biết đến và xây dựng các cuộc tấn công hoạt động không cần con người. Công ty của Sam Altman cho biết, GPT-6 Astra đạt 100% trên ExploitBench - công cụ đánh giá năng lực an ninh mạng tấn công của tác nhân và LLM. Trong một thử nghiệm của công ty, AI mới cũng đã phát hiện hai lỗ hổng zero-day chưa được biết đến.
"Chào mừng đến với kỷ nguyên siêu trí tuệ AGI", Brockman viết. "Với cá nhân tôi, tôi nghĩ OpenAI đã đạt được mục tiêu".
